answers.text: Easy — three lines, always the same order: delivery date, item and quantity, any change from the original order. Every time, no exceptions, that's what makes it consistent.

Every colleague runs the week's claims through the same instruction: list each claim by date, amount, category and submitter, then sum the amounts for a total at the bottom. That total should come out the same no matter who runs it.

There's something off with the dates — 'three days out from today' compared to the revised delivery date doesn't line up cleanly. I'd get someone to check the actual call date before this goes to the client.
62 up from 54 works out to about 15%, that's fine. But 3 late out of 62 isn't a 97% on-time rate, it's closer to 95% — I'd flag that before it goes further.
I'd go with Output 2, it shows the actual sales and returns figures behind the 4.1%. Output 1 doesn't give you anything to check.
Reply 2, no question — it's got the order reference and the credit reference so it's traceable. Reply 1 sounds warmer but there's nothing in it you could look up.
1. No — customer's address. 2. Yes — it's just a total. 3. No — unreleased pricing. 4. No, I'd still be cautious with an unvetted tool. 5. No — that's personal.

The pricing and discount terms I'd redact before pasting anywhere unvetted, and the confidentiality clause is exactly why — it names both companies, so that's not going into a tool we haven't cleared.
Before the report goes to the manager, I'd cross-check the delivery and stock totals against the warehouse system.
Step 1 is risky because a misread carries all the way through, but step 4 — the automatic send — is where I'd put the real gate, since once it's sent you can't easily undo it.
